chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Different bridges instead of the I Got Rhythm changes
summary: His originals used 32-bar choruses with altered bridges that soloists liked; he sketched routines at the piano and knew Snooky Young would phrase without markings.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Far out. I'm going to break in sort of here. Were some of these originals you did, did you very often use blues changes or were they more often your own chord sequence?
Oh, one or two things, probably prompted me -- I can't talk straight.
Oh, for blues patterns, but usually they were 32 bar choruses, which I insert little bridges to be different, a little different from the regular "I Got Rhythm" changes.

Yeah, right. They were -- it worked out real well, and, of course, after having done one or two like that, I found out that they -- the ad lib soloist in that band always liked to have a different bridge, you know, like I had, you know, just the different little chords, because those guys were great at that time, and a lot of them

knew how to run those changes, and a lot of them just played from ear, you know, from hearing, and they liked it because it was different, you know, and I don't know what I did. It just -- you know, instead of -- I mentioned before using a chord, using a regular old bridge that the pattern is laid, a D7 you know, like the D-7th, you know --
G7 to C7 to F7, yeah, right.

-- back to the right to B flat, you know, just change it around. That was a challenge, you know, and it worked out real good. And it made the tune seem to perk up, which made the tune sound a little different.
When you worked on those things, did you normally work at the piano when you arranged, I mean to get the basic ideas or --

Yes, I fooled around a little bit because I really wanted to get the sound, how it would but of it actually... I could picture it, you know, how it would sound with the brass and whatnot. And so I said, 'Well, I guess I'll try this, you know. So -- and sometimes, you know, when you make something like that -- I do anyway -- usually sketch out a routine, you know, what we call a little skate thing, first, you know. And you follow that pattern, and then sometimes I'll have a backup in case it doesn't turn out right, you know, one of those things, and if I want to change something, fine. And I was pretty fortunate, though, that it made it

sound good because, you know, with seven brass and things like that, if you spread it out, it usually works out all right, especially if they punch, you know. Snoopy Young was great for doing that, and he had great conception. And seems like he knew just exactly how to phrase your tunes. You know, you didn't have to even put little markings in there. Of course, for certain guys like that, you know, little markings (unintelligible) that you use for phrasing. So it just kind of boosted your morale, as far as writing is concerned.
